svg.title: Errors list: 71 mistakes found so far in the project's own work, what caught each, and where each stands
svg.desc: A list of 71 errors: 67 in the research, 2 in reviews and 2 in process. 67 are corrected, 3 recorded and not undone, and 1 open.
svg.text: Errors list: 71 mistakes found so far in the project's own work, what caught each, and where
Grouped into research errors, errors in reviews of the work, and process errors. Each row names its date, its kind and what caught it.

Change log (am) said each of 19 found votes approved one law; for the

Change log (am) said the adjudicator settled seven questions; it was
three questions, ruling on seven rows.
Passages written before the addenda to results.md, and the codebook
README's sign counts, still read as current.
The 141 and 137 Basic-Law change counts have no script, and recompute
as 140 and 136 under the stated rule.
The README said critics objected to the Court's power to strike down
Basic Laws, where Medina dates the critique to the Court's 1995
decision (p. 684, footnote 4); the same paragraph paraphrased Medina
more strongly than his text in four places.
A line-by-line check against the article
The plain-language README opening dropped the formula Threat =
Capability × Intent, on which the analyses rest.
The note's evidence item 9 and the 2025 row of matrix M1 say the Court
froze and annulled two dismissals; the cited timeline records that one
was held unlawful after the government had rescinded it, with no
operative order, and only the attorney general's was frozen and
The fresh reader of the figures
The note's evidence item 6 says the simple-majority amendment power
was exploited only from late 2022; p. 708 says in recent years,
especially since the government elected at the end of 2022.
A check of the figures' premises against
The README's glossary said a law showing one warning sign was rushed
through the Knesset; Medina's word is expedited (p. 699).
The fresh reader of the figures
The outcome table qualified the revised T1's Refuted verdict as the
project's operationalization but credited a Supported verdict to Claim
C itself, so T1 could support Medina but never refute him.
C-model's forbidding clause turned on what it means for the Court to
have closed an instrument, which was never defined; undefined, the
clause could not be refuted, though on the class reading it already
Rival R2 was declared refuted on both 2023 amendments by the Court's
own indicators, which cannot test a rival that distrusts the Court's
reasons, and the refutation was said to stand whatever the tests show.
Matrix M1 said intent was low and the amendment power undiscovered
before late 2022; Medina says it was increasingly exploited in recent
The note said purpose is a constraint separate from the sliding scale;
pp. 700 and 708 tie purpose to deviation, and the separation is the
The doctrine matrix made a limited, coalition-only contradiction valid
with a legitimate purpose, against p. 701 and the prediction table,
and placed Human Dignity and Liberty under coalition-only support.
C-doctrine's forbidding clause spoke of an amendment being struck and
omitted p. 701's purpose condition, so it did not match the prediction
The outcome table said the Fisher test separates the weak R5 from the
decision-rule claim; step 15 says the rows that separate them are a
The elite-interest rival was measured by ideology only; a version in
which the Court acts against a governing bloc whatever the content was
Claim A answered Medina's sentence with Hasson's five values rather
than its own list at p. 685, called values checks, and dropped
An identity reading of "very existence" (p. 682) was not considered,
and R-chain rested on a newspaper headline (fn. 9) and on p. 688,
which speaks of identity, not a guarantee.
Item 1 and M1 said reservist refusals and pressure stopped the plan;
Medina says reservists declared they would withdraw, and the
Item 3 said the sliding scale operated as it predicts on the 2024
rulings, from which Medina builds the scale.
T1 revised still said "declared before outcomes" and disclaimed
blindness only for the notorious rows, though the assembler and every
role reported seeing outcomes on other rows.
The restated must-match control could not fail on the blind record,
its result was not reported, and an inference was called a convention
The nine-row run was called pre-registered, though the post-1995
restriction was written after those rows were seen.
The next step named for nine rows, the comparison sample, adds no
primary rows, and the note omitted that the full unit reaches six only
if all five codable rows are discordant.
T2's decision rule covered neither mixed outcomes nor no moves, and
T3 fixed no thresholds, no trigger and no window, though the package
was never enacted and the 2023 amendments were followed by the war.
The note called Claim A the best supported, though no test bears on it
and C-A cannot be tested on the present record.
M3 said extra-legal pressure blocks Basic Law amendments, though both
M2 filed Bergman, an ordinary statute, under Basic Law amendment, and
its appointments cell conflicted with M1's 2025 amendment.
The doctrine matrix said Incapacity was invalid on purpose alone; the
Court deferred it to the next Knesset (p. 701).
The Status line, the R5 row, C-doctrine's six form indicators and
steps 12 and 15 read as if T1 had not run and the blind coders had not
Step 1 said the purpose constraint was first applied in 2017; Medina
gives a 2017 case as one example (p. 699), and the project's notes
The note spoke of the article's cut-off, which no source gives; the
M1's 2025 and 2026 rows held details not in the cited timeline: the
March date, a freeze "at once", no interim orders found, and two
Step 11a was presented as discriminating between the two beneficiary
signs, though on the nine rows it reproduces the first run exactly,
and it left unclear which analysis decides.
The formalisation claimed to make C-doctrine and C-model one thing; it
counts support twice and says nothing about instrument switching.

The sensitivity analysis flipped scope, which enters no prediction,

The ontology cited section 4.2 for the reversibility of threats, and

In the first run, outcomes were delivered with litigation timing, so

A coder's report committed to the repository quoted a local file path.
Not recorded; issue 18 says commits are
Rule: an error is listed if it reached the repository's record (a commit, the change log or an issue), or was made in a review given to the author, and was
later found wrong, whether it has since been corrected, recorded without being undone, or is still open. Each date is the day the error was found. Drafts
corrected before they were committed are not listed. No error recorded so far is a mistranslation; much of the work rests on Hebrew sources read by
language-model readers, so that is not evidence that none has occurred.
Where each was corrected: figures/data/fig7-errors.csv (from figures/sources/errors.csv), which cites the change-log item, commit or issue.
